q: An auditor wants to rely on an automated three-way match control in a client's purchasing system. IT general controls over program changes and access have been tested and found effective for the period. Which approach to testing the automated control is generally appropriate?
choices: Test a sample of 60 transactions throughout the year
Test the control with a small number of instances, often one per relevant condition, because effective ITGCs support consistent operation
Rely on management's inquiry responses alone
Test the control only at year-end with a sample of 25 transactions
exp: Because automated controls perform consistently unless changed, an auditor can test each relevant scenario once when ITGCs over changes and access are effective. Large manual-control sample sizes are unnecessary for a properly controlled automated control.

q: An auditor plans to use a system-generated aging report of accounts receivable to select confirmations. What should the auditor do before relying on the report?
choices: Accept the report because it was produced by the system
Obtain a written representation from the controller that the report is accurate
Obtain evidence about the completeness and accuracy of the report, such as testing the report logic and reconciling its totals to the general ledger
Request the same report from the client's IT department on a different day
exp: Information produced by the entity must be evaluated for completeness and accuracy before it is used as audit evidence (AU-C 500). A management representation complements but cannot replace evidence about the report's reliability.

q: An auditor tests whether terminated employees' system access was removed timely. Which population and procedure provide the most reliable evidence?
choices: Select a sample of active users from the system and ask managers whether they still work at the company
Review the IT department's access removal policy
Inquire of the IT manager about the termination process
Obtain a list of terminated employees from HR, select a sample, and compare termination dates with access removal dates in system logs
exp: Starting from the HR termination list tests the right direction for the control and comparing it with system evidence shows whether removal was timely. Policy review and inquiry address design only and are not sufficient evidence of operating effectiveness.

q: To test the change management control that all production program changes are approved, an auditor should select the sample from which population?
choices: A system-generated list of changes actually migrated to production, such as from the change log or version control system
The list of approved change tickets in the ticketing system
Changes that the IT manager identifies as significant
Emails requesting changes from business users
exp: Selecting from changes actually made in production tests whether every change had approval, including any made outside the ticketing process. Sampling from approved tickets would never reveal unauthorized changes, because they have no ticket.

q: Which type of audit evidence is generally the most persuasive regarding the operating effectiveness of an IT control?
choices: Inquiry of the system administrator
Reperformance of the control by the auditor
A memo from the CIO describing the control
Observation of a control that operates monthly, performed once
exp: Reperformance gives direct, auditor-generated evidence that the control works as designed, and is generally more persuasive than observation or inquiry. Observation is limited to the moment observed, and inquiry alone is never sufficient.

q: An auditor uses generalized audit software to analyze 100% of a client's 2.4 million vendor payments for duplicates, round amounts, and payments to vendors not on the approved list. What is the primary advantage of this approach?
choices: It eliminates the need to understand the client's controls
It eliminates the need to evaluate the reliability of the data
It allows the auditor to examine the entire population and identify anomalies that sampling might miss
It replaces the need for professional judgment in evaluating results
exp: Data analytics enable testing of entire populations and targeting of unusual items. The auditor must still assess the completeness and accuracy of the data extracted and use judgment to investigate exceptions.

q: An auditor processes fictitious test transactions, including some with invalid customer numbers and excessive credit amounts, through the client's live order-entry program to see whether the edits reject them. What technique is being used?
choices: Parallel simulation
Embedded audit module
Generalized audit software
Test data approach
exp: The test data approach runs auditor-prepared transactions through the client's program and compares results with expected outcomes. Parallel simulation instead reprocesses the client's real data using the auditor's own program.

q: An auditor writes a program that independently recalculates the client's payroll using actual payroll input data and compares the results with the client's payroll register. What technique is this?
choices: Parallel simulation
Test data approach
Integrated test facility
Snapshot technique
exp: Parallel simulation reprocesses actual client data with auditor-controlled software and compares outputs. The test data approach uses fictitious transactions in the client's program.

q: A bank's internal auditors created a dummy branch in the production system so they can continuously enter test transactions alongside real ones and compare results with expectations. What is the main risk of this integrated test facility?
choices: It cannot test programmed controls
Test transactions may contaminate live financial data if they are not properly reversed or excluded from reporting
It requires the auditor to have no knowledge of the system
It can be used only on weekends
exp: An ITF mixes fictitious transactions with production data, so they must be carefully isolated and reversed to avoid misstating records. Testing programmed controls in the live environment is precisely its benefit.

q: An auditor obtains a vendor master file extract from the client to perform analytics. The extract shows invoice totals of $4,512,300, while the accounts payable subledger and the general ledger both show $4,530,800. What should the auditor conclude?
choices: The extract is reliable because the difference is less than 1%
The general ledger is overstated by $18,500
The extract appears incomplete or inaccurate by $18,500, so the auditor should investigate and obtain a complete extract before relying on analytics
The difference is immaterial and the analytics can proceed
exp: Reconciling extracted data to the ledger is a key completeness check; a $4,530,800 - $4,512,300 = $18,500 difference means some records may be missing from the population tested. Treating the GL as wrong ignores that it agrees with the subledger.

q: An auditor selected 40 terminated employees and found that 3 still had active ERP access more than 30 days after termination. The auditor's tolerable deviation rate is 5%. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: The control is effective because 3 exceptions is a small number
The control is effective because the sample deviation rate is 5%
The auditor should expand the sample to 400 to dilute the exceptions
The sample deviation rate of 7.5% exceeds the tolerable rate, so the control cannot be relied upon as planned
exp: The sample deviation rate is 3/40 = 7.5%, which exceeds the 5% tolerable rate, so the auditor should not rely on the control as planned and should evaluate the effect on the risk assessment and substantive testing. Expanding the sample to dilute exceptions is not appropriate.

q: An auditor finds that developers at a client have unrestricted access to migrate their own code into production, and no compensating monitoring exists. How does this ITGC deficiency most directly affect the audit?
choices: The auditor may not be able to rely on automated application controls and system-generated reports without additional testing
It has no effect because application controls are tested separately
The auditor must issue an adverse opinion on the financial statements
The auditor can rely on application controls if management states that no unauthorized changes were made
exp: Weak program change controls undermine the assumption that automated controls operated consistently throughout the period, so reliance requires additional procedures or substantive testing. An ITGC deficiency does not automatically lead to an adverse financial statement opinion.

q: A user auditor plans to rely on a SOC 1 Type 2 report covering January 1 through September 30 for an audit of the calendar year. What should the auditor do regarding the October-through-December gap?
choices: Ignore the gap because nine months of coverage is sufficient
Obtain a bridge letter from the service organization and perform additional procedures as needed, such as testing user entity controls, for the uncovered period
Request a SOC 2 Type 1 report instead
Assume controls were ineffective during the gap
exp: A bridge (gap) letter is management's representation about changes after the report period, which the auditor supplements with other evidence based on risk. A SOC 2 Type 1 report addresses different criteria at a point in time and would not fill the gap.

q: A SOC 1 Type 2 report from a payroll processor lists complementary user entity controls (CUECs), including that the user entity reviews payroll registers for accuracy. What is the user auditor's responsibility regarding these CUECs?
choices: None, because CUECs are the service auditor's responsibility
Request that the service organization perform the CUECs
Determine whether the user entity has designed and implemented the relevant CUECs and, if relying on them, test their operating effectiveness
Report the CUECs as deficiencies in the service organization's controls
exp: The service organization's control objectives are achieved only if user entities perform the CUECs, so the user auditor must evaluate them at the client. They are not deficiencies; they are part of the designed control system.

q: A SOC 1 report states that the service organization uses a subservice data center and presents it using the carve-out method. What does this mean for the user auditor?
choices: The subservice organization's controls were fully tested by the service auditor
The user auditor cannot use the report at all
The carve-out method applies only to SOC 2 reports
The subservice organization's controls are excluded from the report, so the user auditor may need other evidence, such as the subservice organization's own SOC report, about relevant controls
exp: Under the carve-out method, the subservice organization's controls are excluded from the description and testing, though complementary subservice organization controls are identified. The inclusive method, by contrast, covers the subservice organization's controls within the report.

q: An auditor observes the client's data center for 30 minutes and sees that the door requires a badge and that visitors sign in. What is the main limitation of this evidence?
choices: Observation provides evidence only at the time observed and may be affected by the auditor's presence
Observation is never acceptable audit evidence
Observation provides evidence about the entire audit period
Observation is more persuasive than reperformance
exp: Observation is limited to the point in time and people may act differently while watched, so it should be supplemented with evidence such as access logs over the period. It is a valid procedure, just limited in scope.

q: During a walkthrough of the sales process, an auditor follows a single transaction from order entry through invoicing and posting to the general ledger, examining documents and system screens. What is the primary purpose of this walkthrough?
choices: To test the operating effectiveness of controls for the full year
To confirm the understanding of the process and evaluate whether relevant controls are designed and implemented
To substantively test the accuracy of revenue
To identify all fraud in the sales cycle
exp: Walkthroughs confirm the auditor's understanding of transaction flows and help evaluate design and implementation of controls. One transaction cannot establish operating effectiveness over the period.

q: Under the risk assessment standards revised by SAS No. 145, what must the auditor do with respect to the client's IT environment?
choices: Test all IT general controls regardless of risk
Rely solely on the client's SOC reports for IT understanding
Obtain an understanding of the IT environment and identify risks arising from the use of IT and the general IT controls that address them, for relevant applications
Exclude IT from the risk assessment if the client uses packaged software
exp: SAS 145 (AU-C 315) requires the auditor to identify IT applications and aspects of the IT environment subject to risks arising from IT, and the related general IT controls. It does not require testing every ITGC regardless of relevance.

q: An auditor tests the client's quarterly user access review for the ERP system. Which procedure provides the best evidence that the review operated effectively?
choices: Inquire of the IT director whether reviews occurred
Read the access review policy
Observe a manager sign the access review form
Inspect a sample of completed reviews for evidence of reviewer sign-off, verify the user listings were complete, and confirm that access flagged for removal was removed
exp: Effective testing confirms that the reviewer used complete data, actually reviewed it, and that identified issues were resolved. A signature alone may indicate a rubber-stamp review if the underlying listing was incomplete or removals were not made.

q: A client's ERP calculates depreciation automatically. To test this calculation, the auditor recomputes depreciation for a sample of assets using the asset cost, useful life, and method in the master file. What procedure is this?
choices: Reperformance
Inquiry
Confirmation
Observation
exp: Independently executing the calculation to verify the system's result is reperformance (recalculation). Confirmation involves obtaining a direct response from a third party.

q: An external auditor plans to use the work of the client's internal audit function in testing IT general controls. Which factor is most important in deciding the extent of such use?
choices: The number of internal auditors on staff
The objectivity and competence of the internal audit function and whether it applies a systematic, disciplined approach
Whether internal audit uses the same audit software as the external auditor
The cost savings to the client
exp: AU-C 610 requires evaluating internal audit's objectivity, competence, and systematic approach before using its work, with the external auditor retaining sole responsibility for the opinion. Fee savings cannot drive the decision.

q: An auditor performs ITGC testing at an interim date covering January through August, for a December year-end. What should the auditor do regarding the remaining period?
choices: Nothing, because interim results apply to the full year
Retest all controls in full at year-end
Obtain evidence about significant changes to the controls since the interim date and perform rollforward procedures appropriate to the risk
Rely on management's representation letter alone
exp: When controls are tested at an interim date, the auditor obtains evidence about changes in the remaining period, with the extent depending on risk and the length of the period. Full retesting is not required unless risks warrant it.

q: An auditor wants to evaluate segregation of duties within a large ERP system with thousands of users and roles. Which approach is most efficient and effective?
choices: Interview each user about their job responsibilities
Review the organizational chart
Inspect printed job descriptions for a sample of employees
Use a data analytics tool to extract user role assignments and compare them with a conflict matrix of incompatible functions
exp: Automated analysis against a conflict rule set evaluates actual system permissions across the entire population. Organizational charts and job descriptions show intended duties but not what the system actually allows.

q: During ITGC testing, an auditor finds that the database administrator also has the ability to approve journal entries in the ERP application. Management has implemented a monthly independent review of all journal entries posted by the DBA. How should the auditor view this review?
choices: As a potential compensating control that, if effective, may mitigate the segregation of duties conflict
As irrelevant because only preventive controls matter
As evidence that the conflict is a material weakness
As a substitute for all other ITGCs
exp: Compensating controls can reduce the risk from a deficiency to an acceptable level if they are precise enough and operate effectively, which the auditor must test. Detective controls can mitigate risk; they are not irrelevant.

q: An auditor relies on a client's system to calculate sales commissions. Which procedure would best establish that the commission rates used by the system are authorized?
choices: Inquire of the sales manager about the rates
Compare the rates in the system's configuration table with approved commission plans and inspect evidence of authorization for changes to the table during the period
Observe a salesperson receive a commission check
Recalculate total commissions as a percentage of total sales
exp: Comparing the configured rates with approved source documents and testing changes to those settings directly addresses authorization. An overall ratio may look reasonable even if individual rates are unauthorized.

q: When testing whether a client's financial reporting system logs all changes to vendor bank account details, what is the auditor's primary concern about relying on the audit log?
choices: That the log is printed in a readable format
That the log is longer than one page
That the log is complete and protected from modification or deletion by the users whose activity it records
That the log was reviewed by external auditors in prior years
exp: An audit log is reliable evidence only if logging cannot be disabled or altered by the users being monitored. If administrators can edit the log, it may not capture unauthorized changes.

q: An auditor identifies a deficiency in an IT general control. Which consideration is most relevant in evaluating its severity?
choices: Whether the ITGC deficiency was caused by an outsourced provider
How many hours IT staff spent remediating the deficiency
Whether the CIO agrees with the finding
Whether the deficiency could lead to a misstatement through the automated controls, reports, or data that depend on the ITGC, and whether compensating controls exist
exp: ITGC deficiencies are evaluated based on their effect on the application controls and information they support, considering compensating controls. Management's agreement does not determine severity.

q: Which situation is most appropriate for a dual-purpose test?
choices: Inspecting a sample of sales invoices for evidence of credit approval while also verifying the invoice amounts agree with shipping documents and posted revenue
Observing a data center door during a walkthrough
Inquiring of IT staff about backup procedures
Reviewing the IT strategic plan
exp: A dual-purpose test uses the same sample to test a control (credit approval) and obtain substantive evidence (accuracy of recorded amounts). The other procedures gather only understanding or control evidence.

q: An IT auditor needs to determine whether password parameters in the ERP system meet the company's policy. Which evidence is most reliable?
choices: The written password policy
A screenshot of the password settings obtained directly by the auditor from the system, or observed being generated
A spreadsheet prepared by the IT manager summarizing the settings
An email from the help desk confirming compliance
exp: Evidence obtained directly by the auditor from the system is more reliable than information compiled by client personnel. A manager's summary spreadsheet could contain errors or omissions.

q: An auditor wants to verify that the client's ERP prevents posting of journal entries to closed periods. Which procedure provides the best evidence?
choices: Ask the controller whether closed-period postings are possible
Read the month-end close checklist

In a test environment confirmed to mirror production configuration, or by inspecting the production configuration, verify the period-close setting and attempt or observe a posting to a closed period being rejected
Count the number of journal entries posted in the period
exp: Inspecting the configuration and observing the system rejecting a test posting provides direct evidence of an automated preventive control. Inquiry and checklists do not show how the system actually behaves.

q: During an audit, the IT manager provides an export of user accounts generated two days earlier. What should the auditor do to ensure the listing is reliable?
choices: Accept the listing because it is recent
Ask the IT manager to sign the listing
Compare the listing to the prior year's listing
Observe the listing being generated from the system or generate it directly, and verify its parameters, so the population is complete and unaltered
exp: Observing or obtaining the extraction directly reduces the risk that the population was manipulated or filtered. A signature attests to nothing about whether accounts were removed from the file.

q: Management plans to remediate an ITGC deficiency identified in the third quarter by implementing a new access provisioning process in November. For an integrated audit of internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, what must the auditor do to conclude the remediated control is effective at year-end?
choices: Test the new control for a sufficient period of operation before year-end to obtain evidence it is operating effectively
Accept management's statement that the control was implemented
Test only the old control
Wait until the following year to test the new control
exp: A remediated control must operate for a sufficient period, and be tested, for the auditor to conclude it is effective as of the assessment date. Management's assertion alone is insufficient evidence.

q: An auditor uses an embedded audit module that continuously flags and records transactions over $50,000 processed by the client's payment system. What is the main advantage of this technique?
choices: It requires no involvement in system design
It enables continuous monitoring of transactions as they are processed, providing evidence in a system with no paper trail
It eliminates the need for ITGC testing
It allows the auditor to change production data
exp: Embedded modules capture selected transactions in real time for later review, which supports continuous auditing in paperless environments. They must be built into the application and still depend on effective change controls.

q: An auditor's documentation of IT controls testing states only 'Tested access controls; no exceptions.' What is the primary deficiency in this documentation?
choices: It is too long
It should have been prepared by the client
It does not identify the items tested, procedures performed, evidence obtained, and conclusions reached in enough detail for an experienced auditor to understand the work
It fails to include the auditor's opinion on the financial statements
exp: Audit documentation standards (AU-C 230) require sufficient detail for an experienced auditor with no previous connection to the engagement to understand the nature, timing, extent, and results of procedures. A bare conclusion does not meet this standard.

q: An auditor plans to test an automated control that calculates interest on customer loans. The ITGCs were not tested this year. What is the most appropriate approach?
choices: Test one instance of the control and rely on it for the full year
Rely on last year's ITGC testing without further procedures
Assume the control is ineffective and perform no testing
Either test the relevant ITGCs or obtain other evidence that the control operated consistently, such as testing it at multiple points or performing more substantive procedures
exp: Testing one instance of an automated control is sufficient only when ITGCs provide evidence it did not change; otherwise the auditor needs other evidence of consistent operation. Prior-year ITGC results alone do not cover changes during the current year.

q: An auditor learns that the client's IT department has performed an upgrade of the general ledger application during the year. What is the most relevant audit procedure?
choices: Obtain evidence that data was completely and accurately converted, and that relevant automated controls and reports were tested and approved after the upgrade
Ignore the upgrade if it was performed by the software vendor
Rely on the vendor's marketing materials describing the upgrade
Request that the upgrade be reversed
exp: System upgrades and data conversions create risks that balances were not transferred correctly and that controls changed, so the auditor tests conversion reconciliations and post-upgrade control functioning. Vendor involvement does not remove these risks.

q: An auditor needs to determine whether a client's daily automated interface between the billing system and the general ledger transfers all transactions. Which procedure provides the best evidence?
choices: Inquire of the billing manager whether the interface works
Inspect a sample of interface reconciliations comparing record counts and control totals between the billing system and the GL, including resolution of differences
Review the interface's design document only
Recalculate a single invoice
exp: Reconciliations of record counts and totals between systems, with evidence that differences were investigated, test both completeness and accuracy of the interface. A design document shows intent, not operation.

q: An auditor finds that a client's ERP generates a sales cutoff report using parameters entered by the user each time it is run. What should the auditor do to rely on this report?
choices: Rely on the report because it is system generated
Test only the report's formatting
Test the report logic and also verify the parameters entered when the report was run, such as dates and entities selected
Recalculate the report total only
exp: User-entered parameters can alter what a report includes, so the auditor must verify that the correct parameters were used in addition to testing the report's logic. Recalculating the total does not prove the report captured the right transactions.
